title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: how far it went, and what came of it

questions.prompt: The little word "so" does four different jobs in English, and only one of them is the pattern this lesson teaches: a degree named, and the result that degree produced. Tick EVERY sentence that does that job.

options.text: The path was so steep that the mules refused to go a step further.
The river had risen in the night, so the village was cut off for two days.
She was so patient with the little ones that no one heard her raise her voice.
He learned to swim that summer, and so did both of his sisters.
The wind on the terrace was so cold that evening!

questions.explanation: Look for two things together: an adjective measured by so, and a that-clause reporting what came of that measurement. Steepness produces a refusal to climb, and patience produces a voice never raised, so both belong to the lesson. The river sentence has no adjective under so at all: the word sits between two clauses and merely links them, telling you that one followed the other without saying how far anything went. The swimming sentence uses so in its third job, where it means that the same is true of somebody else. And the terrace sentence does measure a degree, but it stops there and never says what the cold brought about — it is an exclamation, and that is why it needs no that.

questions.prompt: Join these two ideas in one sentence with the pattern of this lesson: "The lorry driver felt great fear." + "He did not leave his cab for a whole hour." Which line is right?

options.text: The driver had so fear that he did not leave his cab for a whole hour.
The driver felt so a great fear that he did not leave his cab for an hour.
The driver was so frightened that he did not leave his cab for an hour.
The driver was so frightened, so he did not leave his cab for an hour.

questions.explanation: The difficulty is hidden in the first idea, which hands you a noun where the pattern needs an adjective. Nothing can be done with the noun itself, so it has to be converted before the sentence will take it, and the verb changes with it: felt fear becomes was frightened. Two of the wrong lines keep the noun and try to force it in, once bare and once with its article dragged along behind so, and neither is English. The fourth line converts the noun correctly and then throws the pattern away at the joint, replacing the tie with a second so, which links the halves without measuring anything — the very thing you were asked to do.

questions.prompt: Read this story. "For eleven years Habib mended watches in a shop no wider than a door. One winter a customer left a gold pocket watch to be cleaned and never came back for it. Habib advertised twice and wrote to the address on the repair slip, and no answer ever reached him. When the shop was sold he gave the watch to the town museum, with the slip still folded inside it. Three years later the customer's daughter found it in a glass case there." Which of these is a summary of it?

options.text: A customer left a gold watch with a watchmaker and never came back for it. The watchmaker advertised twice and wrote to the address on the repair slip, and no answer reached him.
A watchmaker kept a gold watch a customer had left and never collected. He looked for the owner in vain, gave it to the museum when his shop closed, and the owner's daughter found it there.
A watchmaker worked eleven years in a shop no wider than a door, in a town with a museum and glass cases. Gold watches were rare there, and repair slips were folded into the cases.
A greedy watchmaker held on to a gold watch that was not his for years, and parted with it only when his shop was sold and the thing was of no more use to him at all.

questions.explanation: A summary has to reach the end. Only one of these four crosses the whole story: what the watchmaker was left with, what he tried, where the watch went, and how it was found again. Another version is accurate as far as it goes and then stops at the point where the trouble has only just begun, which is the commonest way of losing marks on this exercise. A third keeps the small pleasures of the text — the width of the shop, the glass cases — and lets every event slip through, so that after reading it you still do not know what happened. And the fourth adds a word the story never gave you: nothing there says the man was greedy, and a summary that judges has stopped summarising.

questions.prompt: A pupil hands in this paragraph as a narrative. "Sofiene has grown tomatoes on the same two hectares since he left school. He rises at four, waters until seven, and drives to the market every Friday. His neighbours come to ask his advice about seed. Last month the co-operative gave him a certificate, and he keeps it above the door where everyone who comes in can see it." His teacher writes underneath: this is not yet a story. What is missing?

options.text: a setting that says where these events happen and when
characters the reader can follow from one line to the next
a closing line that leaves the reader with something
an event that upsets the calm and starts the story off

questions.explanation: Read the paragraph again and count what it already has. It has a place and a stretch of time, it has a man you can follow and neighbours around him, and it ends on a line that settles rather than breaks off. What it does not have, anywhere, is a moment when something goes wrong. Nothing threatens the two hectares, nobody disputes the advice, the certificate arrives and is hung up. Without that break there are no episodes to arrange, no tension to raise and nothing to resolve, which is why the paragraph is a portrait and not a narrative: it describes a life instead of telling what happened to it.

questions.prompt: Read this short story. "Nabil opened his sister's letters for a year, telling himself that he was protecting her. He learned nothing that could harm her and warned her of nothing. When she found out she said very little; she simply began posting her letters from the office instead. They still eat at the same table, and she still tells him about her week in the same voice as before, and he no longer believes a word of it." Nobody in the story ever states what it is about. What is its theme?

options.text: that letters on paper are safer than messages sent by telephone
that a suspicion acted on destroys the trust it claimed to protect
that a brother read his sister's letters for a year and was found out
that a family which eats at one table will forgive anything in the end

questions.explanation: Ask what would still be true if the letters were replaced by a telephone, the brother by a colleague and the house by an office. Everything about a watcher who ends up unable to believe the person he watched would survive that move, and that is the mark of a theme. What the brother did and how he was caught would not survive it, because those are the events themselves — the plot, not what the plot is for. The safety of paper is a detail of the story taken for its point. And the last reading is contradicted by the closing line: they are still at the same table, and precisely nothing has been forgiven.

questions.prompt: Here is a passage and the notes a pupil took from it. "When the water rose, the ferryman refused to cross before dawn. The apothecary, who had waited at the bank since midnight, paid a boy to carry his bag along the shore on foot. The boy reached the far village by six, and the sick man lived." One line of the notes gives an act to the wrong person. Which line?

options.text: the ferryman — refused to cross the water before dawn
the apothecary — paid a boy to carry the bag for him
the apothecary — reached the far village by six o'clock
the boy — walked along the shore carrying the bag

questions.explanation: Notes of this kind are only as good as the subject attached to each verb, and one subject here has been quietly swapped. The apothecary hires and pays; it is the boy who walks and the boy who arrives, and the whole point of the passage is that the man who needed to cross never crossed at all. Three lines survive the check: the refusal belongs to the ferryman, the hiring to the apothecary, the walk to the boy. The mistake is easy to make because the apothecary is the person the passage is most concerned with, and a hurried reader gives the important character every verb in sight.
